evidence.text: The patient had no history suggestive of complete statin intolerance and also denied partial statin intolerance, having previously tolerated statin therapy without recurrent limiting adverse effects. There was no established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease documented. A diagnosis of heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia had been present. Despite ongoing statin therapy in combination with other lipid-lowering drugs, LDL-C treatment targets were not met, with an LDL-C value of 160 mg/dL on the current regimen. In planning ongoing lipid-lowering management, simvastatin was not selected at a dose above 20 mg/day, while pravastatin was planned at 80 mg/day. The primary clinical focus was management.

condition: Does the child/adolescent with asthma have ABPA?
patient: A child with asthma was evaluated and did not appear to have poorly controlled disease, as symptoms were controlled on appropriate therapy with moderate- to high-dose inhaled corticosteroids plus a long-acting beta-agonist, with the diagnosis considered correct, adherence and inhaler technique adequate, comorbidities appropriately managed, and environmental triggers addressed. Despite this, the clinical course was consistent with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The patient had not previously received systemic glucocorticoid therapy specifically for ABPA and was therefore treatment-naïve. When systemic corticosteroid treatment was planned, the overall oral steroid course was not intended to extend beyond 16 weeks including tapering. The initial regimen was not started as a low-dose prednisolone/prednisone-equivalent 0.5 mg/kg/day for the first 2 weeks; instead, an initial dose of 0.75 mg/kg/day was used. Management.

patient: An adult patient with known cirrhosis was evaluated in the outpatient setting. The patient was not asymptomatic yet considered at elevated risk for hepatic encephalopathy, as there was no evidence presented of decompensated cirrhosis or prior covert hepatic encephalopathy. The primary clinical focus was management.

condition: Is eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m² AND does the patient have a mutation consistent with pyridoxine responsiveness?
patient:
The patient presented with clinical and biochemical features raising suspicion for primary hyperoxaluria. Kidney function was markedly reduced, with an estimated GFR of 22 mL/min/1.73 m², consistent with advanced chronic kidney disease (stage 4). Because of suspected primary hyperoxaluria in the setting of eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², genetic testing for primary hyperoxaluria types 1–3 was obtained within 30 days of presentation, and plasma oxalate was also measured given the presence of CKD stage 4 or higher.

Genetic testing established primary hyperoxaluria type 1. The patient was treated with pyridoxine, and biochemical assessment of pyridoxine responsiveness was performed; however, there was not full pyridoxine responsiveness, as urinary oxalate remained above the upper reference limit of normal at 62 mg/24 h while on pyridoxine. Despite eGFR remaining <30 mL/min/1.73 m², the identified genotype was not consistent with pyridoxine responsiveness and was also not consistent with pyridoxine unresponsiveness.

The primary clinical focus was management.

condition: Is there no ongoing clinical disease (no ongoing stone disease/nephrocalcinosis/renal impairment)?
patient:
The patient was evaluated for suspected primary hyperoxaluria on clinical and biochemical grounds. Kidney function was preserved, with an estimated GFR of 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Two separate 24-hour urine collections demonstrated hyperoxaluria, with oxalate excretion of 75 mg/day and 78 mg/day (upper reference limit 40 mg/day). Enteric and other secondary causes were excluded, with no evidence of fat malabsorption or an enteric source to explain the elevated oxalate.

Genetic testing was performed and confirmed primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1). Pyridoxine responsiveness was then assessed with repeat urinary oxalate measurements after more than 2 weeks of pyridoxine; oxalate decreased from a mean of 76.5 mg/day pre-treatment to a mean of 52 mg/day on pyridoxine, representing a reduction of approximately 32%, but urinary oxalate did not normalize and remained above the upper reference limit. Urinary oxalate excretion remained markedly elevated at 1.9 times the upper reference limit. There were no features of an active clinical phenotype, with no ongoing stone disease, nephrocalcinosis, or renal impairment documented, and it was also not the case that there was no ongoing clinical disease.

Primary clinical focus: management.
